segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this I saw another angel coming down from heaven. He had great authority, and the earth was lit up by his glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he cried out with a mighty voice, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place of demons, a prison for every unclean spirit, a prison for every unclean bird, and a prison for every unclean and hated beast,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: because all the nations have fallen by the wine of the passion of her prostitution, and the kings of the earth prostituted themselves with her, and the merchants of the earth grew rich from the power of her luxury.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I heard another voice from heaven saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come out of her, my people, so that you do not share in her sins and do not receive any of her plagues,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for her sins have piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Pay her back as she herself has paid, and pay her double for what she has done; in the cup she mixed, mix her a double measure.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her that much torment and mourning. For in her heart she says, ‘I sit as a queen; I am no widow, and mourning I will never see.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire, for mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the kings of the earth, who prostituted themselves with her and lived in luxury with her, will weep and beat their breasts over her when they see the smoke of her burning,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: standing far off for fear of her torment, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon the mighty city! For in a single hour your judgment has come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargo any more,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: cargo of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls, and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet, and every kind of citron wood and every article of ivory and every article of the most precious wood and bronze and iron and marble,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and cinnamon and spice and incense and perfumed oil and frankincense, and wine and olive oil and fine flour and wheat, and cattle and sheep, and horses and carriages and slaves—and human lives.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The ripe fruit your soul craved has gone from you, and all that was rich and splendid is lost to you, and never again will they be found.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The merchants of these things, who grew rich from her, will stand far off for fear of her torment, weeping and mourning,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: For in a single hour such great riches have been laid waste.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And every helmsman and everyone who sails for any port, and sailors and all who make their living from the sea, stood far off

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and cried out as they watched the smoke of her burning, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What city is like the great city?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they threw dust on their heads and cried out, weeping and mourning, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, the great city, where all who had ships at sea grew rich from her wealth! For in a single hour she has been laid waste.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice over her, heaven, and you holy ones and apostles and prophets, for God has given judgment for you against her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then a mighty angel picked up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “So, with violence, will Babylon the great city be thrown down, and she will never be found again.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: The sound of harpists and musicians and pipers and trumpeters will never be heard in you again; no craftsman of any craft will ever be found in you again; the sound of a mill will never be heard in you again;

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: the light of a lamp will never shine in you again; the voice of bridegroom and bride will never be heard in you again. For your merchants were the magnates of the earth, for all the nations were led astray by your sorcery,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: and in her was found the blood of prophets and holy ones, and of all who have been slaughtered on the earth.”

notes.phrase: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!
notes.note: The cry echoes Isaiah 21:9. The whole chapter is built from the prophets' dirges over ancient Babylon and over the trading city of Tyre (Isaiah 13, 23 and 47; Jeremiah 50–51; Ezekiel 26–28). A first-century reader steeped in the Septuagint would have heard those oracles being reapplied to the great city of the preceding chapter.

The Greek word ordinarily means a prison or guard-post, and it means prison elsewhere in Revelation (2:10; 20:7). Most translations soften it to ‘haunt’ because the background in Isaiah pictures ruins inhabited by wild creatures. The ordinary sense is kept here: the fallen city is where unclean things are confined, though ‘lair’ or ‘haunt’ remains a common scholarly reading.

notes.phrase: a prison for every unclean and hated beast
notes.traditional: a cage of every unclean and hateful bird
notes.note: The manuscripts differ over how many items stand in this list. Some have only spirits and birds, others spirits and beasts, others all three; the shorter forms probably arose when a copyist's eye skipped between the repeated phrases. The edition translated here prints all three, while some critical editions bracket the clause about beasts as doubtful.

The Greek words for ‘have fallen’ and ‘have drunk’ differ by a single letter, and the manuscripts are divided. ‘Have fallen’ has strong early support and is the reading of the edition translated here. Many editors and most translations prefer ‘have drunk’ because it suits the image of wine and matches 14:8 and 17:2.

The Greek word is the same one translated ‘Gentiles’ elsewhere in the New Testament. It means a people or nation, and in the plural often means the non-Jewish peoples. In Revelation's phrase ‘all the nations’ the scope is the whole world, so ‘nations’ is used.

The word can mean either intense passion or anger, and elsewhere in Revelation it usually refers to God's wrath. Here it may describe the intoxicating passion of Babylon's prostitution, or the wrath that her prostitution brings down on those who drink. Translations are divided; the first reading is followed.

The noun and its verb (‘prostituted themselves’) share a root with the word for the prostitute who personifies the city in chapter 17, and the rendering keeps that link visible. The image comes from the prophets, who described a city's corrupting alliances and trade as prostitution (for example Isaiah 23:17 of Tyre). Most translations use ‘fornication’, ‘sexual immorality’ or ‘adulteries’; the sense is figurative in any case.

The voice is not identified. ‘My people’ suggests God or Christ, and the call echoes Jeremiah 51:45, yet the voice goes on to speak of God in the third person (verses 5 and 8), so it may be an angel speaking on God's behalf. It is also uncertain where the speech ends: it is closed here at verse 8, but some interpreters run it through verse 20.

The word rendered ‘slaves’ is literally ‘bodies’, the ordinary commercial term for slaves in the Greek of the period. The closing phrase, literally ‘souls of people’, is the Septuagint's expression for human beings traded as merchandise (Ezekiel 27:13). Placed at the end of the cargo list, it may simply restate ‘slaves’ or may add a pointed comment that these goods are human lives.

notes.phrase: The ripe fruit your soul craved has gone from you
notes.note: The Greek turns without warning to address Babylon directly, and no speaker is named. Some translations put the verse in the merchants' mouths, and others treat it as part of the heavenly voice that began in verse 4. It is left here, like verse 20, as an unattributed address, without quotation marks.

‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God's people’.

notes.phrase: given judgment for you against her
notes.traditional: God hath avenged you on her
notes.note: The Greek is compressed, literally ‘God has judged your judgment from her’. It may mean that God has upheld their case against her, or that God has exacted from her the sentence she once passed on them. The rendering follows the first reading, which is the more common, but the second is well supported.

candidates.reason: The πορν- word group recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation, and translators vary between fornication, sexual immorality, prostitution and adultery; Revelation's figurative use needs to stay tied to the word for the prostitute.
It occurs throughout the New Testament with senses ranging over life, self, person and soul, and an unguided choice between ‘soul’ and ‘life’ will vary from chapter to chapter.
It is frequent in Revelation alongside ὀργή, and the choice among wrath, fury and passion, and how to distinguish it from ὀργή, should be fixed once.
It recurs in the Gospels, the letters and Revelation, where translators alternate between deceive, mislead and lead astray for the same sense.
It is used in the Gospels and Revelation both as denunciation and as lament, and translations vary between woe, alas and how terrible, so readers lose the link between passages.
